title: Architecting the Data Layer for AI Agents: From Transactional Systems to MCP and Semantic Models
gist: TOTVS's Fabiane Nardon lays out a production playbook for feeding enterprise data to AI agents: split logic between deterministic code and probabilistic LLMs along precision/security/cost lines, back MCP tools with data-mesh 'data products' and Semantic Web ontologies for governance and disambiguation, add a low-latency Postgres/DuckDB tier for agent-speed retrieval, and squeeze token costs with an MCP Fabric pattern, dynamic tool search, and leaner response formats like CSV and TOON.

insights.claim: Enterprise AI application success depends on deliberately deciding which functionality is handled by deterministic code versus probabilistic LLM reasoning, with that decision driven by a tradeoff across precision, security, and cost.
insights.speaker: Fabiane Nardon
insights.so_what: Vendors and enterprises selling 'agentic' products should be evaluated on where they draw this deterministic/non-deterministic line, not just on model quality -- it's the actual driver of reliability and cost.
insights.quote: The success of your application depends on knowing where to draw the line between the two computational models, what you should send to the deterministic part of the software, and what you should send to GenAI or LLM models.
insights.locator: Deterministic and Non-Deterministic Computational Models

insights.claim: Enterprise transactional systems are traditionally held to roughly 99.99% precision, but AI agents using probabilistic reasoning cannot reach that same precision level, forcing enterprises to redesign workflows and user expectations around irreducible imprecision.
insights.speaker: Fabiane Nardon
insights.so_what: Enterprise buyers of agentic software should expect and budget for a permanent precision gap versus legacy transactional systems, not treat it as a bug to be eliminated.
insights.quote: We're never going to have the same level of precision we have in transactional systems, and we have to deal with that.
insights.locator: opening remarks on enterprise-grade agents

themes.theme: Sourcing data for agents: transactional systems vs. data platform

insights.claim: TOTVS, whose enterprise software runs roughly a quarter of Brazilian GDP, found that its core obstacle in building AI agents was not a lack of data but the fact that its existing data -- built for applications (transactional systems) or for dashboards and analysts (data lakes) -- had never been structured for access by token-hungry, latency-sensitive AI agents capable of firing hundreds of unpredictable queries in minutes.
insights.speaker: Fabiane Nardon
insights.so_what: Any large enterprise with mature transactional/analytics systems should expect a dedicated data-re-platforming effort before agents can be deployed reliably, regardless of how good the underlying data already is.
insights.quote: our problem was not lack of data, it was the opposite. We had too much data and none of it was prepared to be accessed by agents.
insights.locator: opening remarks, TOTVS background

insights.claim: TOTVS's rule for where agents should read data: go directly to the transactional system (ERP/CRM) only for write operations, when data freshness cannot tolerate delay, or to fire business rules coded into that system; otherwise route through the data platform, which is used for stale-data-tolerant workflows, historical processing, semantic search, and data enrichment from external sources.
insights.speaker: Fabiane Nardon
insights.so_what: Gives architects a concrete decision rule for agent data routing rather than defaulting everything to either the live database or a data lake copy.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'You should reach the transactional system when'

insights.claim: Connecting AI agents directly to legacy transactional systems creates operational risk because those systems are often not built to absorb large volumes of unpredictable queries, lack the compute for historical processing, contain uncleaned/noisy data, and frequently lack native semantic (vector) search support.
insights.speaker: Fabiane Nardon
insights.so_what: Explains why enterprises copying data to a separate agent-serving platform is becoming standard practice rather than optional infrastructure.
insights.locator: paragraph on primary source of data / transactional systems

themes.theme: Data mesh and MCP tool governance

insights.claim: TOTVS designed its MCP tools so that each tool maps one-to-one to a 'data product' in its data mesh architecture, meaning every MCP tool automatically inherits an owner, a stable interface contract, documentation, discoverability, and a quality SLA, which solves the governance problem of not knowing who owns or is responsible for a proliferating set of AI tools.
insights.speaker: Fabiane Nardon
insights.so_what: Offers a reusable governance pattern for any enterprise scaling past a handful of MCP tools: tie tool ownership to existing data-mesh domain ownership instead of building new governance from scratch.
insights.quote: if you connect the MCP tools to the data product, you have this governance automatically just by using the same architecture.
insights.locator: paragraph on designing MCP tools with data products

insights.claim: TOTVS deliberately replaced generic MCP tools (like get_schema and generate_query) with specific, business-oriented tools built by the data-product owner who knows the underlying business rules, arguing this produces more precise and safer data retrieval than letting the LLM infer schema and generate its own queries.
insights.speaker: Fabiane Nardon
insights.so_what: A concrete argument against the 'give the LLM raw schema access' pattern many teams default to when standing up MCP servers.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Now instead of doing generic tools'

themes.theme: Semantic Web ontologies as the fix for LLM ambiguity

insights.claim: Different departments in the same company never converge on a single definition of basic business concepts (e.g., what counts as an 'active customer' differs between marketing and finance), and unlike humans who resolve this ambiguity through social/contextual familiarity, LLMs and AI agents lack that sensibility and need the ambiguity resolved explicitly in the data layer.
insights.speaker: Fabiane Nardon
insights.so_what: Enterprises deploying agents across departments should expect semantic conflicts between business units to surface as agent errors unless definitions are formally disambiguated.
insights.quote: The problem is not having multiple definitions, it's pretending there's only one.
insights.locator: paragraph on 'active customer' definitional conflict

insights.claim: TOTVS solves cross-department semantic ambiguity for its AI agents using 25-year-old Semantic Web standards -- RDF for giving each business concept a unique identifier, and OWL ontologies for encoding relationships between concepts -- originally proposed by Tim Berners-Lee in a 2001 Scientific American article envisioning agents that understand each other well enough to coordinate tasks like scheduling medical treatment.
insights.speaker: Fabiane Nardon
insights.so_what: A 25-year-old, largely dormant W3C technology stack (RDF/OWL) is being repurposed as core AI-agent infrastructure -- a signal that 'old' semantic-layer standards may see fresh enterprise demand driven by LLM adoption.
insights.quote: he described a world where agents can talk to each other and understand each other, and they could organize and solve people's problems.
insights.locator: paragraph on Tim Berners-Lee's 2001 Scientific American article

insights.claim: Nardon argues that Semantic Web technology only became practically usable now because current LLMs have been trained on 25 years of examples of RDF and OWL, whereas when she did her own PhD in Semantic Web technologies 20 years ago, the biggest obstacle was the sheer manual labor of building an ontology -- a task LLMs can now do quickly given existing documentation.
insights.speaker: Fabiane Nardon
insights.so_what: Suggests a broader pattern worth watching: previously 'failed' or stalled technology standards (not just Semantic Web) may become newly viable once LLMs can absorb their formalisms and automate the costly manual-authoring step.
insights.quote: it took us 25 years to get to a point where you can actually use this technology to solve the semantic problem.
insights.locator: paragraph on PhD in Semantic Web Technologies

insights.claim: In a live demo using plain ChatGPT with no special training, feeding the model an OWL ontology that classified 'server' as a subclass of 'cloud service' (not hardware) changed its answer to the question 'which customers bought hardware' compared to when no ontology was provided, showing an explicit ontology can override an LLM's default (and potentially wrong) inference.
insights.speaker: Fabiane Nardon
insights.so_what: Concrete, replicable proof point that off-the-shelf LLMs (not just fine-tuned or RAG-heavy systems) respond correctly to formal ontology injection, lowering the bar for enterprises to try this pattern.
insights.locator: ChatGPT servers/hardware ontology demo

insights.claim: A 2024 study found that adding an ontology-based semantic layer improved LLM response precision by 40% compared to plain LLM use on the same data, with more recent studies showing even higher correctness gains depending on data formatting and domain.
insights.speaker: Fabiane Nardon
insights.so_what: A quantified, citable ROI figure (40% precision lift) that investors and buyers can use to evaluate vendors claiming semantic-layer or knowledge-graph enhancements to LLM pipelines.
insights.quote: they proved that adding an ontology-based semantic layer improved LLM response precision by 40%.
insights.locator: paragraph citing 2024 study

themes.theme: Low-latency, multi-tier data platform for agents

insights.claim: TOTVS's data platform runs three distinct latency tiers behind one unified processing interface: a high-latency Apache Spark layer for batch processing of Parquet files, a medium-latency Google BigQuery layer for large-volume but costlier processing, and a low-latency layer built on Postgres and DuckDB purpose-built to serve AI agents.
insights.speaker: Fabiane Nardon
insights.so_what: A concrete reference architecture for any enterprise data platform team retrofitting existing Spark/BigQuery pipelines to serve real-time agent workloads without ripping out prior investment.
insights.locator: paragraph on data platform toolbox / three layers

insights.claim: TOTVS built its low-latency Postgres/DuckDB serving layer roughly two years before this talk specifically to support AI agents, ahead of Databricks' more recent announcement that it would support Postgres -- suggesting TOTVS anticipated a data-platform architecture shift that larger vendors are only now formalizing.
insights.speaker: Fabiane Nardon
insights.so_what: A smaller enterprise player being ahead of a major data-platform vendor (Databricks) on this specific architecture choice is a signal that low-latency Postgres-style serving layers for agents may become a broader industry standard, not a TOTVS-specific quirk.
insights.quote: We've been doing this for two years, more or less, just because we needed to serve agents, and we need to have a low latency option.
insights.locator: paragraph referencing Databricks Postgres support

insights.claim: TOTVS's low-latency pipeline uses long-standing Postgres features -- triggers that fire stored procedures -- to atomically transform and load raw data the instant it lands, prioritizing guaranteed consistency and simplicity over newer, more fashionable streaming tools.
insights.speaker: Fabiane Nardon
insights.so_what: Counters the assumption that agent-ready data infrastructure requires exotic new tooling; well-understood relational-database primitives can still solve the freshness/consistency problem at lower risk and cost.
insights.quote: I know it's not fancy, but it works very well.
insights.locator: paragraph on Postgres trigger-based pipeline

insights.claim: Serving AI agents requires two distinct kinds of low latency that legacy data platforms built for dashboards were not designed to deliver: fast data processing (time from data ingestion to being query-ready) and fast data retrieval (time to serve that data back to the agent), and TOTVS designed its architecture to be vendor-neutral, low-cost, fast, reliable, and semantic-search capable specifically to meet both.
insights.speaker: Fabiane Nardon
insights.so_what: Gives infrastructure buyers a two-part checklist (processing latency and retrieval latency) for evaluating whether an existing data platform is actually agent-ready.
insights.locator: paragraph on why low latency matters for agents

themes.theme: Security: embedding access control in tools, not prompts

insights.claim: TOTVS deliberately rejected the popular approach of a generic database tool that lets the LLM read the schema and write its own queries, because that pattern is highly vulnerable to prompt injection; instead it uses narrow, parameterized tools with security logic embedded directly in tool code, trading flexibility (an agent can only access data a tool explicitly exposes) for materially lower prompt-injection risk.
insights.speaker: Fabiane Nardon
insights.so_what: A direct, practitioner-tested counter-argument to 'let the LLM generate SQL' architectures being sold as flexible -- relevant for any investor evaluating AI-data-access startups on security posture, not just capability.
insights.locator: Security section, paragraph on generic tools vs. parameterized tools

insights.claim: TOTVS propagates the logged-in user's identity from its company identity provider through OAuth tokens into every MCP tool call, so per-user data filtering (e.g., 'only show employees this logged-in user manages') happens automatically at the tool layer rather than being left to the LLM to reason about or enforce.
insights.speaker: Fabiane Nardon
insights.so_what: A reusable identity-propagation pattern (OAuth token carries logged user into every tool call) for enterprises that need row-level or role-based access control on agent-served data.
insights.locator: paragraph on identity provider and OAuth propagation

themes.theme: Token cost economics and MCP Fabric

insights.claim: Because purchasing power in Brazil is far lower than in the US, a tool priced at '$100' like Claude Code effectively costs TOTVS the equivalent of $500 -- about a third of the Brazilian minimum wage -- meaning token costs became an acute forcing function for TOTVS's architecture choices years before token-cost concerns became a mainstream industry discussion.
insights.speaker: Fabiane Nardon
insights.so_what: Emerging-market enterprises may be a leading indicator for token-efficiency techniques (dynamic tool search, compact serialization formats) that developed-market companies will only adopt once dollar-denominated token costs bite harder.
insights.quote: when you say that Claude Code costs only $100 bucks, for us it's $500 bucks. This is a third of the Brazilian minimum wage.
insights.locator: Cost section, opening remarks on Brazil and token economics

insights.claim: TOTVS built a pattern it calls 'MCP Fabric,' implemented using Spring AI, that serves many virtual MCP servers as distinct URLs from a single running service, allowing them to spin up hundreds of per-agent MCP servers without paying the deployment cost of running a separate service for each one.
insights.speaker: Fabiane Nardon
insights.so_what: A named, reusable infrastructure pattern ('MCP Fabric') that reduces the operational/deployment cost of proliferating MCP servers -- relevant for any platform team scaling agent tooling.
insights.locator: Cost section, paragraph introducing MCP Fabric

insights.claim: TOTVS's internal benchmark comparing dynamic tool search against loading every tool definition into context (tested at 10, 25, 50, and 100 tools) showed that token consumption from putting all tools in context grows substantially faster than with dynamic tool search, which instead has the agent query a separate search_tool service (using semantic search, Lucene, or regex) to retrieve only a handful of relevant tool candidates on demand.
insights.speaker: Fabiane Nardon
insights.so_what: Quantifies a specific, implementable technique (dynamic tool search/retrieval instead of static tool-list injection) for cutting token spend as an agent's available tool count scales into the hundreds.
insights.locator: paragraph on dynamic tool search benchmark chart

insights.claim: Switching MCP tool response formatting from JSON to flat CSV can cut token usage by up to 50% for tabular data, and a newer, purpose-built format called TOON can save 30% to 60% of tokens versus JSON for mixed tabular/complex data, though TOON currently costs some precision because LLMs have far more training exposure to JSON and CSV than to TOON.
insights.speaker: Fabiane Nardon
insights.so_what: A concrete, low-effort lever (response serialization format) for cutting agent token costs, with TOON flagged as an early-stage format worth watching but not yet a precision-safe default.
insights.quote: TOON can represent also mixed tabular data and complex data, and can save 30% to 60% tokens in the result.
insights.locator: paragraph on JSON vs. CSV vs. TOON

insights.claim: Asked whether a more compact serialization like Protocol Buffers could replace JSON/TOON for tool responses, Nardon said the deciding factor is not raw compactness but how well the LLM was trained to interpret a given format -- JSON's ubiquity in training data lets models parse it with less ambiguity than newer or less common formats, a tradeoff TOTVS is still actively testing.
insights.speaker: Fabiane Nardon
insights.so_what: Warns technical buyers not to choose a data-serialization format purely on token-efficiency benchmarks; a format's representation in the LLM's training data can matter more for real-world precision.
insights.quote: The LLM usually can understand better JSON with less ambiguity than TOON.
insights.locator: Q&A, Participant 1 on Protocol Buffers

insights.claim: TOTVS partially manages RDF/ontology entity-deduplication problems -- where the same real-world concept can end up with different identifiers -- by organizing ontology creation along the same domain and data-product boundaries used in its data mesh, so each domain team is responsible for its own slice of the shared ontology rather than one team trying to unify everything.
insights.speaker: Fabiane Nardon
insights.so_what: Ontology/knowledge-graph deduplication is described as an unsolved, ongoing 'art' rather than a solved problem -- a caution for anyone assuming semantic layers are turnkey once built.
insights.locator: Q&A, Participant 2 on deduplication

insights.claim: At TOTVS, either data-product teams or agent-building teams can create new MCP tools -- in practice it is a mix, since whichever team has direct access to the needed data and understands the business schema typically ends up owning tool creation, with tools frequently built by one domain team and reused by a different team building an unrelated agent.
insights.speaker: Fabiane Nardon
insights.so_what: Shows that cheap, fast MCP tool creation (via TOTVS's data platform tooling) blurs the traditional data-team/application-team boundary, which is an organizational, not just technical, consequence of good agent-data tooling.
insights.locator: Q&A, Participant 4 on who creates tools
